---
title: "What Changes When You Swap the Factors?"
description: "Compare the nonzero eigenspaces of AB and BA, then use the smaller product to compute powers of a Markov transition matrix."
categories: ["Linear Algebra", "Probability"]

## Two Products, Two Sizes

Take a column and a row:

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The product $AB$ is the $2\times2$ diagonal matrix with entries $1,0$. The product $BA$ is the $1\times1$ matrix $(1)$. Both have eigenvalue $1$, while only $AB$ has eigenvalue $0$.

This agreement away from zero holds in general. As in [the note on rectangular inverses](rectangular-matrix-inverses.qmd), the sizes help us keep track of the maps. If $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times m$, then $P=AB$ acts on $m$ coordinates, and $Q=BA$ acts on $n$.

## How the Eigenspaces Match

For a square matrix $M$, the $\lambda$-eigenspace is $E_\lambda(M)=\{v:Mv=\lambda v\}$. Every nonzero vector in it is scaled by $\lambda$ when we apply $M$. The argument also works for complex eigenvalues by allowing complex vectors.

Associativity gives

$$
PA=AQ,\qquad QB=BP.
$$

Thus if $Qu=\lambda u$, then $P(Au)=\lambda Au$. Multiplication by $A$ sends $E_\lambda(Q)$ into $E_\lambda(P)$. In the other direction, if $Pv=\lambda v$, then $Q(Bv)=\lambda Bv$.

When $\lambda\ne0$, we can undo these maps after a rescaling. For $u\in E_\lambda(Q)$ and $v\in E_\lambda(P)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{\lambda}BAu&=\frac{1}{\lambda}Qu=u,\\
A\frac{1}{\lambda}Bv&=\frac{1}{\lambda}Pv=v.
\end{aligned}
$$

So $A$ and $B/\lambda$ are inverse linear maps between the two eigenspaces. The eigenspaces have the same dimension. In particular, each nonzero eigenvalue of either product is also an eigenvalue of the other.

At zero, this inverse construction breaks down. In the opening example, $AB$ kills $(0,1)^\top$ and $B$ kills it too. There is no nonzero vector for that direction to map to under $B$.

## Computing Powers with the Smaller Product

The factors inside a power of $AB$ can be grouped into copies of $BA$. For instance, $(AB)^2=A(BA)B$. More generally,

$$
(AB)^k=A(BA)^{k-1}B\qquad(k\ge1).
$$

At $k=1$, the middle factor is $Q^0=I_n$. If $P^k=AQ^{k-1}B$, multiplying by $P$ gives

$$
P^{k+1}=AQ^{k-1}(BA)B=AQ^kB.
$$

When $n<m$, this replaces powers of an $m\times m$ matrix with powers of an $n\times n$ matrix.

## A Three-State Markov Example

Use the factors

$$
\begin{aligned}
A&=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\\[.3em]
B&=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Each column has nonnegative entries that sum to one. Therefore each factor maps a probability column vector to another probability column vector. The products are

$$
P=AB=\frac14\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\2&2&2\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix},
$$

$$
Q=BA=\frac14\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Both products are transition matrices. Starting with a distribution $x$ on three states, the formula for $P^k x$ has three steps. First apply $B$ to get a distribution on two states. Next apply $Q^{k-1}$. Finally apply $A$ to return to three states.

The two directions for $Q$ are $(1,1)^\top$ and $(1,-1)^\top$. The first stays fixed. The second is multiplied by $1/2$ at each step. Any two-state probability vector has a fixed part $u=(1/2,1/2)^\top$, so $Q^{k-1}Bx$ tends to $u$. Hence

$$
\lim_{k\to\infty}P^kx
=Au=\frac14\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

This limit is the same for every three-state starting distribution. It is stationary because $P(Au)=AQu=Au$. The two nonzero eigenvalues of $P$ are $1$ and $1/2$. The third is zero since the image of $P$ is contained in the span of the two columns of $A$.

The decay here comes from the factor $1/2$ in the smaller system. [Stationary Does Not Mean Convergent](../probability/stationary-distributions-and-convergence.qmd) uses the same two-state family to show what happens when that factor is $-1$.
